ctx.s: 媒体称这位三十五岁才首次夺冠的选手是{大器晚成}的典型。
ctx.en: The media called the player, who won his first title at thirty-five, a textbook late bloomer.

bad.s: 这座大桥{大器晚成}，比计划晚了两年才通车。
bad.en: (meant: the bridge was finished two years late)
bad.why: It praises a person whose talent is recognised late, not a project that runs behind schedule.

bad.s: 他做作业总是{大器晚成}，每次都最后一个交。
bad.en: (meant: he is always slow and hands in homework last)
bad.why: It is praise for late success in life, not a complaint about being slow or late with a task.

cards.mean: getting better day by day (a business)
cards.lit: rising like steam, higher every day

use.how: Predicate of a business, career, economy or organisation: 生意蒸蒸日上。 Common in good wishes: 祝事业蒸蒸日上。

near.diff: 日新月异 is rapid change, as in technology or a city's look; 蒸蒸日上 is steadily growing prosperity.

cards.cue: A bakery that opened two years ago keeps getting more customers and has just opened a second shop. How is its business doing?

ctx.s: 他开的小饭馆生意{蒸蒸日上}。
ctx.en: The little restaurant he opened is doing better and better.

ctx.s: 自从换了新经理，公司的业绩{蒸蒸日上}。
ctx.en: Since the new manager came in, the company's results have been rising steadily.

ctx.s: 新年快乐，祝贵公司事业{蒸蒸日上}！
ctx.en: Happy New Year, and may your company go from strength to strength!

ctx.s: 这个小镇靠发展旅游业，经济{蒸蒸日上}。
ctx.en: By developing tourism, the town's economy is thriving more every year.

ctx.s: “最近店里怎么样？”“托您的福，{蒸蒸日上}！”
ctx.en: "How's the shop lately?" "Thanks to you, better every day!"

ctx.s: 几年前还濒临倒闭的工厂，如今一派{蒸蒸日上}的景象。
ctx.en: The factory that was close to closing a few years ago is now flourishing.

bad.s: 今天的气温{蒸蒸日上}，热得受不了。
bad.en: (meant: the temperature keeps rising today)
bad.why: Despite the steam image it is not about heat; it describes a business or career that keeps prospering.

bad.s: 最近城里的犯罪率{蒸蒸日上}。
bad.en: (meant: the crime rate keeps going up)
bad.why: It is praise for something flourishing; it cannot describe a bad thing increasing.

cards.mean: built up bit by bit over time
cards.lit: accumulated day by day, piled up month by month

use.how: Used alone as a clause, as an attribute (日积月累的经验) or with 下来; about knowledge, skill, habits or problems built up over a long time. It takes no object.

near.diff: 积少成多 stresses small amounts adding up to a lot; 日积月累 stresses the long stretch of time it takes.

cards.cue: Your friend asks how you got so fluent. You say there was no trick: just a little every day for years.

ctx.s: 词汇量要靠{日积月累}，不能指望一天背完。
ctx.en: Vocabulary grows slowly over time; you can't expect to learn it all in one day.

ctx.s: 他的经验是多年{日积月累}下来的。
ctx.en: His experience was built up over many years.

ctx.s: 这些小毛病{日积月累}，最后变成了大问题。
ctx.en: These small faults piled up over time and finally became a big problem.

ctx.s: 河口的这片沙洲，是泥沙{日积月累}冲积而成的。
ctx.en: The sandbank at the river mouth was formed by silt laid down little by little over a very long time.

ctx.s: “你的字怎么写得这么好？”“没什么诀窍，就是十几年{日积月累}的功夫。”
ctx.en: "How is your handwriting so good?" "No secret, just the skill built up over more than ten years."

ctx.s: 两个人之间的矛盾是{日积月累}的，不是一次吵架造成的。
ctx.en: The tension between them built up over a long time; it wasn't caused by one argument.

bad.s: 我昨天一个晚上就{日积月累}了很多知识。
bad.en: (meant: I learned a lot in one evening)
bad.why: It means building up over months and years, so it contradicts a single evening.

bad.s: 我要{日积月累}钱，将来买房子。
bad.en: (meant: I want to save up money to buy a house)
bad.why: It cannot take an object; say you save little by little, or that the money was built up over time.

cards.mean: a green newcomer, just starting out
cards.lit: just come out of the thatched cottage

story.text: Liu Bei went three times to the thatched cottage where the young Zhuge Liang lived in retirement before Zhuge agreed to serve him. Soon after, Cao Cao's army attacked, and at Bowang Zhuge Liang laid an ambush with fire and routed it. The novel's verse calls this his first achievement on coming out of the thatched cottage, and the phrase came to mean anyone just starting out.

use.how: Attribute (初出茅庐的年轻人) or predicate, about a person new to a job, field or society; often modest when said of oneself.

near.diff: 乳臭未干 scornfully calls someone a mere child; 初出茅庐 neutrally says they are new and inexperienced.

cards.cue: On his first day at a law firm, a fresh graduate tells the partners modestly that he knows he still has everything to learn.

ctx.s: 我刚毕业，{初出茅庐}，还有很多东西要学。
ctx.en: I've only just graduated and I'm brand new; I still have a lot to learn.

ctx.s: 别看他{初出茅庐}，这次的方案做得很漂亮。
ctx.en: He may be new, but he did a beautiful job on this proposal.

ctx.s: 那时候她还是个{初出茅庐}的小记者，什么都不懂。
ctx.en: Back then she was a green young reporter who knew nothing.

ctx.s: {初出茅庐}的年轻人难免犯错，多给他们一些机会吧。
ctx.en: Newcomers are bound to make mistakes; give them a few more chances.

ctx.s: “这个项目交给新人行吗？”“他虽然{初出茅庐}，但很肯学。”
ctx.en: "Can we give this project to a new hire?" "He's inexperienced, but he's eager to learn."

ctx.s: 这位导演{初出茅庐}，第一部作品就获了大奖。
ctx.en: The director was a complete newcomer, yet his very first film won a major award.

bad.s: 这款新手机{初出茅庐}，卖得很好。
bad.en: (meant: the new phone has just come out and sells well)
bad.why: It describes a person new to work or society, not a product that has just been released.

bad.s: 退休多年的老教练这次{初出茅庐}，再次带队参赛。
bad.en: (meant: the old coach came out of retirement)
bad.why: It means a beginner's first steps, not a veteran's return; a comeback calls for a different idiom.

cards.mean: to gain new insight by reviewing the old
cards.lit: to warm up the old and come to know the new

story.text: Confucius said: one who keeps reviewing what he has already learned and gains new understanding from it is fit to be a teacher. The saying became the classic Chinese statement that real learning comes from going back over old material, not only from adding more.

use.how: Predicate or advice, about studying, rereading books or looking back at history and finding something new in it: 读史可以温故知新。

near.diff: 熟能生巧 is practice turning into skill; 温故知新 is review turning into new understanding.

cards.cue: Rereading a novel you studied at school, you notice things you never saw at sixteen.

ctx.s: 考试前把旧笔记再看一遍，可以{温故知新}。
ctx.en: Going over your old notes before the exam helps you see things afresh.

ctx.s: 这本书我读了三遍，每次都能{温故知新}。
ctx.en: I've read this book three times and find something new each time.

ctx.s: 老师常说：“学习要{温故知新}，不要学了新的就忘了旧的。”
ctx.en: The teacher often said: "Learn by reviewing the old to understand the new; don't forget the old as soon as you learn something new."

ctx.s: 重读历史，往往能{温故知新}，看清今天的问题。
ctx.en: Rereading history often brings new insight and helps us see today's problems clearly.

ctx.s: 教练经常带队员重看以前的比赛录像，{温故知新}，找出新的改进办法。
ctx.en: The coach often has the players rewatch old match videos, going back over the old to find new ways to improve.

ctx.s: 他退休后重新翻开大学课本，{温故知新}，竟有了不少新的体会。
ctx.en: After retiring he reopened his university textbooks and, to his surprise, gained many new insights.

bad.s: 我今天{温故知新}，学了一个全新的软件。
bad.en: (meant: today I learned something completely new)
bad.why: It requires going back over what you already know; learning brand-new material is not reviewing the old.

bad.s: 他很{温故知新}，总是怀念过去的日子。
bad.en: (meant: he is nostalgic)
bad.why: It is about learning, not nostalgia, and it cannot be modified by hen like an adjective.

cards.mean: to infer the rest from a single example
cards.lit: shown one, come back with three

story.text: Confucius described how he taught: he did not explain until a student was struggling to understand, and if he lifted up one corner of a subject and the student could not come back with the other three corners, he did not repeat the lesson. From this image of one corner of a square implying the other three comes the idiom.

use.how: Predicate, often after 能/要/学会, about applying one example or lesson to similar cases; in official language also 'apply a lesson to all similar cases'.

near.diff: 融会贯通 is integrating a whole field into full understanding; 举一反三 is extending one example to similar cases.

cards.cue: Shown how to solve one kind of problem, a pupil solves five different variations of it without any help.

ctx.s: 这孩子很聪明，教他一道题，他就能{举一反三}。
ctx.en: This child is clever: teach him one problem and he can work out the rest.

ctx.s: 做数学题不要死记答案，要学会{举一反三}。
ctx.en: Don't memorise answers in maths; learn to apply one method to similar problems.

ctx.s: 老师讲完例题，让我们{举一反三}，自己做后面的练习。
ctx.en: After going through the example, the teacher had us apply it ourselves to the exercises that followed.

ctx.s: “这种新题型你怎么也会？”“跟上次那道差不多，{举一反三}嘛。”
ctx.en: "How can you do this new type of question?" "It's like the one last time; you just extend it."

ctx.s: 好的培训不是教会员工每一种情况，而是让他们能{举一反三}。
ctx.en: Good training doesn't cover every case; it teaches staff to work out new cases from what they know.

ctx.s: 这次事故提醒我们要{举一反三}，把其他工厂的安全隐患也查一遍。
ctx.en: This accident reminds us to apply its lesson widely and check the other factories for hazards too.

bad.s: 我{举一反三}了很多例子来说明我的观点。
bad.en: (meant: I gave many examples to support my point)
bad.why: Ju here does not mean 'give an example'; the idiom means working out many cases from one, and takes no object.

bad.s: 他说话总是{举一反三}，同一件事讲好几遍。
bad.en: (meant: he repeats himself)
bad.why: It praises the ability to generalise, not repeating something several times.

cards.mean: to master a subject by pulling it all together
cards.lit: to melt things together and run a thread through them

use.how: Predicate, often 把……融会贯通 or 做到融会贯通, about knowledge, theories or skills integrated into a deep, unified understanding.

near.diff: 举一反三 is extending one example to similar cases; 融会贯通 is joining a whole body of knowledge into one understanding.

cards.cue: After years of separate courses in grammar, history and literature, a student suddenly sees how they all fit into one picture.

ctx.s: 学过的知识要{融会贯通}，才能真正用起来。
ctx.en: What you've learned has to come together as a whole before you can really use it.

ctx.s: 他把中西医的理论{融会贯通}，形成了自己的方法。
ctx.en: He brought Chinese and Western medical theory together into his own method.

ctx.s: 读了几十本历史书以后，她终于能把各个朝代的事{融会贯通}了。
ctx.en: After dozens of history books, she could finally connect all the dynasties into one picture.

ctx.s: “怎样才算真正学会一门语言？”“语法、词汇和发音都能{融会贯通}的时候。”
ctx.en: "When have you really learned a language?" "When grammar, vocabulary and pronunciation all work together for you."

ctx.s: 这门课的目的是让学生把前三年学的内容{融会贯通}。
ctx.en: This course aims to help students integrate everything from the first three years.

ctx.s: 老教授讲课从不看讲稿，对各派理论早已{融会贯通}。
ctx.en: The old professor never looks at notes; he has long since mastered every school of theory as one whole.

bad.s: 这两家公司{融会贯通}，合并成了一家。
bad.en: (meant: the two companies merged)
bad.why: It is about understanding knowledge as a whole, not organisations merging; just say they merged.

bad.s: 这条路{融会贯通}，可以直达机场。
bad.en: (meant: the road runs straight through to the airport)
bad.why: Running through here is mental, not physical; it describes mastering a subject, not a road connecting places.

cards.mean: vast in scope and profound (a culture or field)
cards.lit: broad and great, refined and deep

use.how: Predicate or noun phrase (……的博大精深) about a culture, language, body of thought or field of learning, never about a person.

near.diff: 见多识广 describes a person who has seen a lot; 博大精深 describes a culture or field that is vast and deep.

cards.cue: After a year studying calligraphy, you realise each stroke has centuries of theory behind it and you have barely begun.

ctx.s: 中国文化{博大精深}，一辈子也学不完。
ctx.en: Chinese culture is so vast and deep you could never finish learning it in a lifetime.

ctx.s: 他越研究中医，越觉得它{博大精深}。
ctx.en: The more he studies Chinese medicine, the more profound he finds it.

ctx.s: “一个‘打’字有这么多用法？”“哈哈，汉语就是这么{博大精深}。”
ctx.en: "The word da has this many uses?" "Ha, that's how deep Chinese is."

ctx.s: 这部著作内容{博大精深}，值得反复阅读。
ctx.en: This work is vast and profound and deserves to be read again and again.

ctx.s: 茶道看似简单，其实{博大精深}。
ctx.en: The art of tea looks simple, but it is actually a vast and subtle field.

ctx.s: 参观完博物馆，外国游客纷纷感叹中华文明的{博大精深}。
ctx.en: After visiting the museum, the foreign visitors marvelled at the depth and breadth of Chinese civilisation.

bad.s: 我的老师{博大精深}，什么都懂。
bad.en: (meant: my teacher is very learned)
bad.why: It describes a culture or field, not a person; for a learned person use a different idiom.

bad.s: 这个房间{博大精深}，能住十个人。
bad.en: (meant: the room is very spacious)
bad.why: Great and deep are not physical size here; it praises the depth of a culture or body of knowledge.

cards.mean: widely experienced and knowledgeable
cards.lit: having seen much, knowing widely

use.how: Predicate or attribute about a person whose knowledge comes from wide experience and travel: 见多识广的老人。

near.diff: 博大精深 describes a culture or field; 见多识广 describes a person who has seen and experienced a lot.

cards.cue: A retired sea captain who has sailed to fifty countries is never surprised by anything you tell him.

ctx.s: 我爷爷年轻时走过很多地方，{见多识广}。
ctx.en: My grandfather travelled to many places when he was young and has seen a lot of the world.

ctx.s: 你{见多识广}，帮我看看这块玉是真是假？
ctx.en: You've seen so much; can you tell me if this jade is real?

ctx.s: 当了二十年记者，她早已{见多识广}，什么场面都不怕。
ctx.en: After twenty years as a reporter she has seen it all and nothing fazes her.

ctx.s: “这种怪事你见过吗？”“我也算{见多识广}了，还真没见过。”
ctx.en: "Have you ever seen anything this strange?" "I've seen a lot, but never this."

ctx.s: 多出去旅行，人会变得{见多识广}。
ctx.en: Travel more and you'll become more worldly and knowledgeable.

ctx.s: 村里人遇到难事，都去请教那位{见多识广}的老船长。
ctx.en: When villagers face a problem, they all go to ask the worldly old captain.

bad.s: 这本书{见多识广}，内容很丰富。
bad.en: (meant: this book covers a lot)
bad.why: It describes a person's experience of the world, not a book's content; say the book's content is rich.

bad.s: 他视力很好，很远的东西也能{见多识广}。
bad.en: (meant: his eyesight is good and he can see far)
bad.why: Seeing here means life experience, not eyesight; the idiom is about knowledge gained from seeing the world.

cards.mean: short-sighted, not thinking ahead
cards.lit: one's gaze is short and shallow

use.how: Predicate or attribute about a person or decision that ignores the future for present gain: 目光短浅的做法。 Not about eyesight.

near.diff: 井底之蛙 is a narrow view from limited experience of the world; 目光短浅 is failing to look ahead to the future.

cards.cue: A company cuts all research spending just to make this quarter's profits look good. How would critics describe the decision?

ctx.s: 只顾眼前利益，不考虑以后，太{目光短浅}了。
ctx.en: Thinking only of immediate gain and not of the future is far too short-sighted.

ctx.s: 为了省钱砍掉培训经费，是一种{目光短浅}的做法。
ctx.en: Cutting the training budget to save money is a short-sighted move.

ctx.s: “他为了一点奖金就跳槽了。”“我觉得他有点{目光短浅}。”
ctx.en: "He changed jobs for a small bonus." "I think that was a bit short-sighted of him."

ctx.s: 当年嘲笑网购没有前途的人，现在看来实在是{目光短浅}。
ctx.en: Those who once laughed that online shopping had no future look truly short-sighted now.

ctx.s: 村民们当初{目光短浅}，砍光了山林卖钱，如今连水都不够用。
ctx.en: The villagers were short-sighted and cut down the forests for cash; now they don't even have enough water.

ctx.s: 父亲常提醒我：做人不能{目光短浅}，要看得远一点。
ctx.en: My father often reminded me not to be short-sighted, but to look further ahead.

bad.s: 我{目光短浅}，看不清黑板上的字。
bad.en: (meant: I'm near-sighted and can't read the board)
bad.why: It is about poor foresight, not eyesight; for eyes use the ordinary word for near-sighted.

bad.s: 他{目光短浅}，做事特别踏实。
bad.en: (meant: he focuses on practical things and works steadily)
bad.why: It is a criticism of ignoring the future, never praise for being down to earth.

cards.mean: to take only a hurried, superficial look
cards.lit: to look at flowers from a galloping horse

story.text: The Tang poet Meng Jiao failed the imperial examination several times and finally passed in middle age. In his joy he wrote the poem 'After Passing the Examination', with the lines: 'Proud in the spring breeze, my horse's hooves fly; in a single day I see all the flowers of Chang'an.' The rider who sees a whole city's flowers in a single day gave the idiom its image; it later came to mean a hasty look that takes in only the surface.

use.how: Adverbial or predicate, often with 地 or 式: 走马观花地看了看. Said of visits, reading or inspections that stay on the surface; often self-deprecating.

near.diff: 浮光掠影 describes a shallow impression or understanding; 走马观花 describes the hurried way of looking or visiting itself.

cards.cue: You have one afternoon for an enormous museum and can only rush past the halls. How do you describe your visit?

ctx.s: 时间太紧，这次去北京只能{走马观花}地看看。
ctx.en: Time is too tight; on this trip to Beijing I can only have a quick look around.

ctx.s: 博物馆这么大，半天只能{走马观花}，下次再来细看吧。
ctx.en: The museum is so big that half a day only allows a quick walk-through; let's come back another time and look properly.

ctx.s: 很多旅行团一天跑五个景点，游客只能{走马观花}。
ctx.en: Many tour groups rush through five sights a day, so the tourists only get a fleeting look.

ctx.s: “那本书怎么样？”“我只是{走马观花}翻了一遍，说不上来。”
ctx.en: "What's that book like?" "I only flicked through it quickly, so I can't really say."

ctx.s: 领导下基层调研，不能{走马观花}，要坐下来听听老百姓的想法。
ctx.en: When leaders go down to do fieldwork, they mustn't just skim the surface; they need to sit down and hear what ordinary people think.

ctx.s: 他{走马观花}地看了一遍合同就签了字，结果吃了大亏。
ctx.en: He gave the contract a quick once-over, signed it, and ended up badly burned.

bad.s: 他学习非常认真，每篇课文都{走马观花}地读。
bad.en: (meant: he studies seriously and reads every text carefully)
bad.why: It means looking hastily and superficially, the opposite of careful reading.

bad.s: 他看问题很快，{走马观花}就能抓住重点。
bad.en: (meant: he is quick and grasps the key point at a glance)
bad.why: It criticises a superficial look; it is not praise for quick, sharp insight.

cards.mean: plain for all to see
cards.lit: everyone who has eyes has seen it together

use.how: Predicate, often in 是……的: 他的进步是有目共睹的. Said of achievements, efforts or changes that no one can deny, usually positive.

near.diff: 众所周知 opens a statement of a fact everyone knows; 有目共睹 says results or changes are visible to all, and is used as a predicate.
显而易见 is a conclusion that is obvious by reasoning; 有目共睹 is something everyone has actually witnessed.

cards.cue: At the year-end meeting, the boss says nobody can deny how much the new hire has improved: everyone has watched it happen.

ctx.s: 这几年家乡的变化是{有目共睹}的。
ctx.en: The changes in my hometown over the past few years are there for all to see.

ctx.s: 她为这个项目付出的努力，大家{有目共睹}。
ctx.en: Everyone has seen how much effort she put into this project.

ctx.s: 经理在会上说：“小王的进步{有目共睹}，今年应该给他升职。”
ctx.en: The manager said at the meeting: "Xiao Wang's progress is plain for all to see; he should be promoted this year."

ctx.s: 这家医院近年来服务水平的提高{有目共睹}。
ctx.en: The improvement in this hospital's service in recent years is evident to everyone.

ctx.s: 公司的产品质量一直很稳定，这是{有目共睹}的事实。
ctx.en: The company's product quality has always been consistent; that is a fact everyone can see.

ctx.s: 他的成绩{有目共睹}，你凭什么说他是靠关系上来的？
ctx.en: His record speaks for itself; what makes you say he got there through connections?

bad.s: {有目共睹}，地球是圆的。
bad.en: (meant: as everyone knows, the earth is round)
bad.why: It cannot open a sentence as 'as everyone knows'; this idiom is a predicate about results everyone has seen.

bad.s: 这个秘密只有我们两个人{有目共睹}。
bad.en: (meant: only the two of us know this secret)
bad.why: It means seen by everyone; it cannot describe something only a few people know or saw.

cards.mean: known to every household
cards.lit: made clear to every family, known in every household

use.how: Predicate or attributive: 这个故事家喻户晓; 家喻户晓的人物. Said of stories, people, songs or brands known to ordinary people throughout a country or region.

near.diff: 举世闻名 is famous across the whole world; 家喻户晓 is familiar to ordinary families within one society.

cards.cue: A character from an old folk tale is so familiar that every grandmother and every child in the country knows his name.

ctx.s: 孙悟空在中国{家喻户晓}，连小孩都知道他。
ctx.en: The Monkey King is a household name in China; even small children know him.

ctx.s: 这首歌一夜之间变得{家喻户晓}。
ctx.en: Overnight, this song became known in every home.

ctx.s: 这个牌子的酱油在我们那儿{家喻户晓}，几乎每家厨房都有一瓶。
ctx.en: This brand of soy sauce is a household name where I'm from; almost every kitchen has a bottle.

ctx.s: 那部电视剧播出以后，演主角的演员成了{家喻户晓}的明星。
ctx.en: After that TV series aired, the lead actor became a household name.

ctx.s: “你没听说过梁山伯与祝英台？这可是{家喻户晓}的故事啊！”
ctx.en: "You've never heard of the Butterfly Lovers? Everybody knows that story!"

ctx.s: 为了让防火知识{家喻户晓}，社区每个月都组织宣传活动。
ctx.en: To make fire-safety knowledge known in every home, the neighbourhood runs an awareness event every month.

bad.s: 这件事我们部门三个人都{家喻户晓}了。
bad.en: (meant: all three people in our department know about this)
bad.why: It describes something known across a whole society, and its subject is the thing known, not the people who know it.

bad.s: 他对历史{家喻户晓}，什么都知道。
bad.en: (meant: he knows everything about history)
bad.why: It says something is widely known, not that a person is knowledgeable. It cannot take the knower as its subject.

cards.mean: world-famous
cards.lit: the whole world has heard its name

use.how: Mostly attributive: 举世闻名的长城; also predicate. Said of places, works, people or products admired worldwide; typical of writing, guides and speeches.

near.diff: 家喻户晓 is known in every home of one society; 举世闻名 is famous across the whole world.
举世瞩目 is the world's attention on an event happening now; 举世闻名 is lasting fame.

cards.cue: A tour guide introduces an ancient monument that visitors from every continent heard of long before they arrived.

ctx.s: 长城是{举世闻名}的古代建筑。
ctx.en: The Great Wall is a world-famous ancient structure.

ctx.s: 景德镇的瓷器{举世闻名}，很多外国游客专门来买。
ctx.en: Jingdezhen porcelain is famous worldwide, and many foreign tourists come specially to buy it.

ctx.s: 导游说：“我们现在看到的，就是{举世闻名}的兵马俑。”
ctx.en: The guide said: "What we're looking at now is the world-famous Terracotta Army."

ctx.s: 这位钢琴家不到三十岁就已经{举世闻名}了。
ctx.en: This pianist was already world-famous before turning thirty.

ctx.s: 谁能想到，这个{举世闻名}的品牌最初只是一家小作坊？
ctx.en: Who would have thought this world-famous brand started out as a small workshop?

ctx.s: 凭着这部小说，他从一个普通教师变成了{举世闻名}的作家。
ctx.en: With this novel he went from an ordinary teacher to a world-famous writer.

bad.s: 我们村的豆腐{举世闻名}，邻村的人都来买。
bad.en: (meant: our village's tofu is well known around here)
bad.why: Its scope is the whole world; it is wrong for fame that reaches only the next village.

bad.s: 这家公司因为造假{举世闻名}。
bad.en: (meant: the company became notorious for fraud)
bad.why: It is admiring fame; it is not used for notoriety earned by wrongdoing.

cards.mean: flashy but lacking substance
cards.lit: flowering but bearing no fruit

story.text: Yang Chufu, a minister of Jin, stopped at the town of Ning on his way home from a mission. The innkeeper, Ning Ying, admired him so much that he left home to follow him, but soon turned back. When his wife asked why, he said Yang was too harsh, and that he flowered but bore no fruit; such a man gathers resentment, and Ning Ying feared he would share in the harm before he gained anything.

use.how: Predicate or attributive: 内容华而不实; 华而不实的人. Criticises people, writing, plans or objects that look impressive but have nothing solid behind them.

near.diff: 中看不中用 is colloquial and mostly about objects that look good but do not work; 华而不实 also judges people, words and plans.

cards.cue: A consultant's proposal has beautiful slides and grand slogans, but not one concrete step anyone could take.

ctx.s: 这个网站做得花里胡哨，有用的信息却没几条，真是{华而不实}。
ctx.en: This website is all bells and whistles, but there's hardly any useful information on it: all show, no substance.

ctx.s: 他的报告写得很漂亮，但内容{华而不实}，没有一个具体办法。
ctx.en: His report is beautifully written, but it is all show with not one concrete measure.

ctx.s: 老师提醒我们：写作文要真诚，不要追求{华而不实}的辞藻。
ctx.en: The teacher reminded us: write sincerely and don't chase showy, empty phrases.

ctx.s: “这个装修方案太{华而不实}了，钱花了不少，住起来却不方便。”
ctx.en: "This renovation plan is all flash and no substance; it costs a lot, but the place would be inconvenient to live in."

ctx.s: 有些年轻人只注重包装自己，难免显得{华而不实}。
ctx.en: Some young people care only about packaging themselves, and inevitably come across as all style and no substance.

ctx.s: 选合作伙伴，我宁要踏踏实实做事的人，也不要{华而不实}的人。
ctx.en: When choosing a partner, I'd rather have someone who works steadily than someone who is all show.

bad.s: 这家餐厅的菜又好看又好吃，真是{华而不实}。
bad.en: (meant: the food looks good and tastes good too)
bad.why: It is a criticism meaning showy but empty; it cannot praise something attractive and substantial.

bad.s: 他穿着很朴素，看起来{华而不实}。
bad.en: (meant: he dresses plainly and looks unpretentious)
bad.why: The first character means showy; plain, modest dress is the opposite.

cards.mean: to make a comeback
cards.lit: to rise again from East Mountain

story.text: Xie An of the Eastern Jin dynasty lived for years in retirement at East Mountain in Kuaiji, turning down every offer of office and spending his time with friends and family. Around the age of forty he finally entered public service, rose to become chief minister, and guided Jin through the war with Former Qin that ended in victory at the Fei River. A return to power after retirement or defeat came to be called rising again from East Mountain.

use.how: Predicate: 他三年后东山再起. Said of a person, team or business that returns to success after failure, defeat or retirement.

near.diff: 卷土重来 is coming back after defeat to try again, and can describe unwelcome things returning; 东山再起 is regaining one's former standing.

cards.cue: A businessman lost everything when his firm went bankrupt; five years later he runs a bigger company than before.

ctx.s: 他生意失败以后没有放弃，三年后又{东山再起}了。
ctx.en: After his business failed he didn't give up, and three years later he made a comeback.

ctx.s: 别灰心，你在这一行的名声还在，总有机会{东山再起}。
ctx.en: Don't lose heart; your reputation in this field is still intact, so there's always a chance to make a comeback.

ctx.s: 这家老字号曾经差点倒闭，没想到靠网上销售{东山再起}。
ctx.en: This old brand nearly went under, but surprisingly it bounced back through online sales.

ctx.s: 记者问：“您退休多年，这次复出是想{东山再起}吗？”
ctx.en: A reporter asked: "You've been retired for years; is this return an attempt at a comeback?"

ctx.s: 这位歌手沉寂了十年，新专辑一出就{东山再起}，又红遍了全国。
ctx.en: After ten quiet years, this singer made a comeback the moment the new album came out, and is famous across the country again.

ctx.s: 他心里清楚，失去了大家的信任，想{东山再起}就难了。
ctx.en: He knew that, having lost everyone's trust, a comeback would be hard.

bad.s: 感冒好了没几天，又{东山再起}了。
bad.en: (meant: a few days after recovering, the cold came back)
bad.why: It is a person or group regaining position, not an illness or problem coming back.

bad.s: 他第一次创业就{东山再起}，赚了很多钱。
bad.en: (meant: his very first business was a big success)
bad.why: A comeback needs an earlier fall or retirement; a first-time success is not a comeback.

cards.mean: unprecedented
cards.lit: what has never existed before

use.how: Mostly attributive with 的: 前所未有的挑战; also predicate. Said of scale, change, feelings or situations never seen before, in the world or in one's own life.

near.diff: 史无前例 is weightier, 'unprecedented in history', for major events; 前所未有 also fits personal experience.

cards.cue: On her first day in charge of the whole team, she feels a pressure unlike anything she has experienced in her life.

ctx.s: 这次考试的难度{前所未有}，很多同学都没做完。
ctx.en: This exam was harder than any before it; many students didn't finish.

ctx.s: 第一次站上这么大的舞台，她感到一种{前所未有}的紧张。
ctx.en: Standing on such a big stage for the first time, she felt a nervousness she had never felt before.

ctx.s: 人工智能给翻译行业带来了{前所未有}的挑战。
ctx.en: Artificial intelligence has brought unprecedented challenges to the translation industry.

ctx.s: “这么热的夏天，在我们这里真是{前所未有}。”
ctx.en: "A summer this hot is unheard of around here."

ctx.s: 搬到乡下以后，他享受到了{前所未有}的安静。
ctx.en: After moving to the countryside he enjoyed a quiet he had never known.

ctx.s: 退休后第一次一个人出国旅行，奶奶觉得{前所未有}地自由。
ctx.en: Travelling abroad alone for the first time after retiring, Grandma felt freer than she ever had.

bad.s: 我们每年春节都举行这个{前所未有}的活动。
bad.en: (meant: we hold this special event every Spring Festival)
bad.why: An event held every year has happened before, so it cannot be unprecedented.

bad.s: 这种情况以前{前所未有}过。
bad.en: (meant: this has never happened before)
bad.why: It already contains 'before' and 'never'; adding 'before' and the experience marker guo again is redundant and ungrammatical.

cards.mean: to waste all the effort already made
cards.lit: all earlier achievement thrown away

story.text: The Qin general Bai Qi had won victory after victory and was about to march past the Zhou domain to attack Liang. The adviser Su Li urged the Zhou ruler to warn him with a story: the archer Yang Youji could hit a willow leaf at a hundred paces, but an onlooker said that if he kept shooting until his arm tired and missed once, all his earlier success would be thrown away. So too Bai Qi: one failed campaign, and his past achievements would count for nothing.

use.how: Predicate, often as a result or warning: 一下午的工作前功尽弃; 现在放弃就前功尽弃了. Said when a slip or setback makes all earlier work count for nothing.

near.diff: 功亏一篑 is failing right at the last step; 前功尽弃 stresses that all the earlier work is wasted, at whatever stage.
半途而废 is choosing to quit halfway; 前功尽弃 is the result, earlier effort wasted, often by a mistake.

cards.cue: Your computer crashes before you save, and an entire afternoon's writing is gone.

ctx.s: 电脑突然死机，文件没保存，一下午的工作{前功尽弃}。
ctx.en: The computer suddenly froze before I saved the file, and a whole afternoon's work was lost.

ctx.s: 减肥最怕半夜吃东西，一顿就可能让你{前功尽弃}。
ctx.en: The danger in dieting is late-night eating; one meal can undo all your efforts.

ctx.s: 妈妈提醒他：“戒烟最难的是头几个月，你现在抽一根，就{前功尽弃}了。”
ctx.en: His mother reminded him: "The first few months of quitting are the hardest; smoke one now and it'll all be for nothing."

ctx.s: 培养了几个月的细菌被污染了，整个实验{前功尽弃}，只能从头再来。
ctx.en: The bacteria cultured for months got contaminated; the whole experiment was wasted and had to start over.

ctx.s: 拼图拼了一个星期，弟弟一碰桌子，全散了，真是{前功尽弃}。
ctx.en: I spent a week on the jigsaw, then my little brother knocked the table and it all fell apart: a week's work for nothing.

ctx.s: 病刚好一点就停药，很容易{前功尽弃}，医生让他一定吃完。
ctx.en: Stopping medicine as soon as you feel a bit better can easily undo the treatment, so the doctor told him to finish it.

bad.s: 他学了三年钢琴，弹得越来越好，真是{前功尽弃}。
bad.en: (meant: three years of piano have paid off)
bad.why: It means earlier effort was wasted; it cannot describe effort that has paid off.

bad.s: 这个项目刚开始，还什么都没做，就{前功尽弃}了。
bad.en: (meant: the project failed right at the start)
bad.why: It needs earlier work to be lost; nothing done means nothing to waste.

cards.mean: worries back home or behind one that hold one back
cards.lit: the worry that makes one look back over one's shoulder

use.how: Noun, usually object of 没有, 解决, 免除: 解决员工的后顾之忧. Said of concerns about family, home or livelihood left behind while one goes off to work, study or fight.

cards.cue: A woman takes a job in another city; her parents promise to look after her child so that she need not worry about home.

ctx.s: 有父母帮忙带孩子，她出国读书就没有{后顾之忧}了。
ctx.en: With her parents helping with the child, she could study abroad without worrying about home.

ctx.s: 学校为参加集训的运动员安排了补课，解决了他们学业上的{后顾之忧}。
ctx.en: The school arranged extra lessons for athletes away at training camp, so they need not worry about falling behind in their studies.

ctx.s: “家里有我，你放心去比赛，不要有{后顾之忧}。”
ctx.en: "I'll take care of things at home; go and compete with your mind at ease."

ctx.s: 孩子没人管，我怎么能在外地安心工作？这就是我最大的{后顾之忧}。
ctx.en: With no one to look after my child, how can I work away from home in peace? That's my biggest worry.

ctx.s: 有了养老保险，他辞职创业时少了一份{后顾之忧}。
ctx.en: With a pension in place, he had one less worry holding him back when he quit to start a business.

ctx.s: 村里办起了托管班，外出打工的父母终于免除了{后顾之忧}。
ctx.en: Once the village set up an after-school care class, parents working in the cities were finally freed from worry about their children.

bad.s: 明天要考试了，我有很多{后顾之忧}，怕考不好。
bad.en: (meant: I'm anxious about tomorrow's exam)
bad.why: It is a worry about what is left behind (home, family, livelihood), not anxiety about what lies ahead.

bad.s: 他是个{后顾之忧}的人，总是想太多。
bad.en: (meant: he is a worrier who overthinks)
bad.why: It is a noun for a specific worry, not an adjective for a personality. It cannot describe what kind of person someone is.

cards.mean: the whole story, the ins and outs
cards.lit: where the dragon comes from and where the vein runs to

story.text: The phrase comes from traditional Chinese geomancy (fengshui). Geomancers likened a mountain range to a dragon and its unbroken ridge to a vein, and when judging a site they spoke of where the dragon came from and where the vein ran on to. The phrase was later extended to the origin and course of any matter.

use.how: Noun, usually 事情的来龙去脉, object of 讲清, 弄清, 了解. Said of the background and full course of an event, problem or idea.

near.diff: 前因后果 stresses cause and effect; 来龙去脉 is the whole course of a matter from its start to where it stands now.

cards.cue: Before judging a quarrel between two colleagues, the manager wants to hear exactly how it started and how it developed.

ctx.s: 你先别生气，听我把事情的{来龙去脉}讲清楚。
ctx.en: Don't get angry yet; let me explain the whole story first.

ctx.s: 警察花了一个星期，才把这笔钱的{来龙去脉}查清楚。
ctx.en: It took the police a week to trace where this money came from and where it went.

ctx.s: “这个词是怎么来的？”“它的{来龙去脉}可复杂了，我慢慢跟你说。”
ctx.en: "Where does this word come from?" "Its history is quite complicated; I'll take you through it."

ctx.s: 新来的同事不了解项目的{来龙去脉}，开会时常常插不上话。
ctx.en: The new colleague doesn't know the project's background, so in meetings he often can't join in.

ctx.s: 这本书详细介绍了丝绸之路的{来龙去脉}。
ctx.en: This book gives a detailed account of the Silk Road from its origins onward.

ctx.s: 只看了一个新闻标题就下结论，你连{来龙去脉}都没搞清楚。
ctx.en: You drew a conclusion from one headline; you don't even know the ins and outs.

bad.s: 他说话很有{来龙去脉}，大家都爱听。
bad.en: (meant: he speaks in a well-organised way)
bad.why: It is a noun for the background and course of a matter, not a quality of speech; it cannot describe how well someone talks.

bad.s: 我昨天把作业的{来龙去脉}都做完了。
bad.en: (meant: I finished every part of my homework yesterday)
bad.why: It means how a matter began and developed, not all the parts of a task.

cards.mean: methodical and unflustered
cards.lit: having threads, and not tangled

story.text: In a speech to his people, the Shang king Pangeng compared good order to a fishing net: when the net is held by its main cord, its strands are in order and do not tangle. That line became the idiom for doing things in an orderly, unhurried way.

use.how: Mostly adverbial before 地 + verb, or as a predicate: 工作进行得有条不紊。 Said of how someone handles tasks, especially under pressure.

near.diff: 井井有条 describes a well-ordered state (a room, accounts); 有条不紊 describes the calm, step-by-step way something is being done.

cards.cue: The fire alarm goes off during an exam; the teacher calmly sends the class out row by row without any panic. How did she handle it?

ctx.s: 她做事一向{有条不紊}，从来不慌。
ctx.en: She always does things calmly and methodically and never panics.

ctx.s: 虽然客人很多，服务员还是{有条不紊}地上菜。
ctx.en: Even with so many guests, the waiters kept serving the dishes in a calm, orderly way.

ctx.s: 停电以后，护士们{有条不紊}地把病人转到了别的楼层。
ctx.en: After the power cut, the nurses moved the patients to other floors calmly and in good order.

ctx.s: 面对记者的提问，新闻发言人{有条不紊}地一一作答。
ctx.en: Faced with the reporters' questions, the spokesperson answered them one by one, calm and methodical.

ctx.s: 婚礼那天乱成一团，多亏你{有条不紊}地安排好了一切。
ctx.en: The wedding day was chaos; thank goodness you calmly arranged everything step by step.

ctx.s: 只剩一个小时了，大家都慌了，只有组长还在{有条不紊}地分配任务。
ctx.en: With only an hour left everyone panicked; only the team leader kept handing out tasks calmly and methodically.

bad.s: 听到坏消息，他{有条不紊}地哭了起来。
bad.en: (meant: he started crying steadily)
bad.why: It describes orderly, methodical handling of tasks, not the manner of an emotional reaction.

bad.s: 我把文件{有条不紊}了。
bad.en: (meant: I put the files in order)
bad.why: It is not a verb that takes an object; to say you sorted the files, use a plain verb meaning tidy up and keep the idiom for the manner.

cards.mean: by the book, following set procedure
cards.lit: to place things by section and put them in their ranks

story.text: The Jin-dynasty writer Lu Ji, describing how a piece of writing is composed, said that the writer chooses ideas and places them in their proper sections, then weighs the words and puts them in their proper ranks. Taken from writing, the phrase came to mean doing anything in its set order, step by step.

use.how: Adverbial (按部就班地做) or predicate. Neutral advice to go step by step, but can criticise rigid routine: 不能再按部就班了。

near.diff: 有条不紊 praises a calm, orderly manner; 按部就班 only says one follows the set steps, and can imply a lack of flexibility.
循序渐进 is gradual progress stage by stage, as in learning; 按部就班 is keeping to an established procedure or routine, sometimes too rigidly.

cards.cue: A new lab assistant wants to skip steps in the standard procedure to save time. You tell him to follow the set procedure exactly, step by step.

ctx.s: 做实验必须{按部就班}，哪一步都不能跳过。
ctx.en: In an experiment you have to follow the procedure in order; you can't skip a single step.

ctx.s: 你先别急，按照说明书{按部就班}地装就行。
ctx.en: Don't rush; just assemble it following the instructions step by step.

ctx.s: 他每天{按部就班}地上班下班，日子过得很平静。
ctx.en: Every day he goes to work and comes home on the same routine, and his life is very quiet.

ctx.s: “这个项目还来得及吗？”“只要{按部就班}地推进，月底前能完成。”
ctx.en: "Can this project still make it?" "As long as we push ahead step by step, it can be done before the end of the month."

ctx.s: 现在情况紧急，不能再{按部就班}了，得想个新办法。
ctx.en: This is an emergency; we can't keep going by the usual procedure, we need a new approach.

ctx.s: 有人批评这家公司过于{按部就班}，缺少创新。
ctx.en: Some people criticise the company for sticking too closely to set routines and lacking innovation.

bad.s: 他突然决定{按部就班}，辞职去旅行了。
bad.en: (meant: he suddenly, on impulse, quit to travel)
bad.why: It means following the set order of steps, the opposite of a sudden impulsive decision.

bad.s: 这个房间收拾得很{按部就班}。
bad.en: (meant: the room is very neatly tidied)
bad.why: It describes going through a process in order, not how tidy a place looks; a neat room calls for a word meaning tidy or well ordered.

cards.mean: to benefit from a misfortune
cards.lit: because of a disaster, to gain good fortune

story.text: Writing about Guan Zhong, the famous chief minister of the state of Qi, the historian Sima Qian said that in governing he was good at turning disaster into good fortune and turning defeat into success. The idea of drawing good out of a misfortune is the core of this idiom.

use.how: Predicate, often after 真是, 算是 or 反而: 他丢了工作，反而因祸得福。 Said after the good outcome has actually come.

near.diff: 塞翁失马 says a loss may turn out well, often as comfort before the outcome is known; 因祸得福 states that the good has already come from it.

cards.cue: A flood shut her shop, so she moved the business online, and sales went up threefold. How do you sum up what happened to her?

ctx.s: 我被裁员以后自己开了店，没想到{因祸得福}。
ctx.en: After I was laid off I opened my own shop, and it unexpectedly turned out to be a blessing.

ctx.s: 他错过了那班飞机，结果{因祸得福}，躲过了一场事故。
ctx.en: He missed that flight, and the mishap saved him: he escaped an accident.

ctx.s: 腿受伤在家的那几个月，她读完了好多书，也算{因祸得福}吧。
ctx.en: In the months she was home with a hurt leg she read lots of books, so you could say some good came of it.

ctx.s: “听说你搬家是因为房东涨租？”“是啊，不过新家离公司更近，真是{因祸得福}。”
ctx.en: "I heard you moved because the landlord raised the rent?" "Yes, but the new place is closer to work, so it turned out a blessing."

ctx.s: 这次失败让团队发现了产品的大问题，可以说是{因祸得福}。
ctx.en: This failure let the team find a major problem in the product, so it was a blessing in disguise.

ctx.s: 那场大病之后，他戒了烟，开始锻炼，反而{因祸得福}，身体比以前更好了。
ctx.en: After that serious illness he quit smoking and started exercising; it actually did him good, and he is healthier than before.

bad.s: 他中了彩票，真是{因祸得福}。
bad.en: (meant: he won the lottery, what luck)
bad.why: There must first be a misfortune that leads to the good; plain good luck such as a lottery win is just luck.

bad.s: 我丢了钱包，真是{因祸得福}，太倒霉了。
bad.en: (meant: I lost my wallet, what bad luck)
bad.why: It means good came out of the bad, not simply bad luck; to complain about losing a wallet, just say it was unlucky.

cards.mean: to escape from the jaws of death
cards.lit: from inside death, to flee into life

use.how: Predicate or object (经历过死里逃生): 他在车祸中死里逃生。 Said of surviving a real mortal danger such as an accident, disaster or war.

near.diff: 九死一生 stresses how deadly the danger or venture was; 死里逃生 stresses the escape itself.

cards.cue: A climber is buried by an avalanche, digs himself out after hours in the snow, and is found alive. What has he just done?

ctx.s: 那次车祸他{死里逃生}，只受了点轻伤。
ctx.en: He narrowly escaped death in that car crash and was only slightly hurt.

ctx.s: 地震时她被困了三天，最后{死里逃生}。
ctx.en: She was trapped for three days in the earthquake and in the end came out alive.

ctx.s: 船翻了以后，几名渔民抱着木板漂了一夜，终于{死里逃生}。
ctx.en: After the boat capsized, several fishermen clung to planks all night and finally escaped with their lives.

ctx.s: “你还记得那次登山遇到雪崩吗？”“怎么不记得，那可真是{死里逃生}啊。”
ctx.en: "Do you remember the avalanche on that climb?" "How could I forget? We barely got out alive."

ctx.s: 报道说，飞行员在飞机坠毁前跳伞，{死里逃生}。
ctx.en: The report says the pilot parachuted out before the plane crashed and escaped death.

ctx.s: 经历过{死里逃生}的人，往往更懂得珍惜生活。
ctx.en: People who have been through a narrow escape from death often value life more.

bad.s: 爷爷昨天{死里逃生}了，我们明天去参加葬礼。
bad.en: (meant: Grandpa passed away yesterday)
bad.why: It means surviving death, the opposite of dying; using it before mentioning a funeral is a shocking contradiction.

bad.s: 我们{死里逃生}地赶上了最后一班车。
bad.en: (meant: we only just caught the last bus)
bad.why: It is about surviving real mortal danger, not being barely in time for a bus, and it is not used as an adverb with the particle de.

cards.mean: a hopeful new way opening when all seemed lost
cards.lit: willows dark, flowers bright

story.text: The Song poet Lu You, walking through the countryside, wrote that among the folded hills and winding streams he began to doubt there was any road ahead, when beyond the shady willows and bright flowers another village appeared. The couplet is still quoted for a sudden way out of an impasse.

use.how: Predicate (事情柳暗花明了) or in the full line 柳暗花明又一村. Said of a turn for the better after an apparent dead end.

near.diff: 苦尽甘来 is a long hardship ending and good times arriving; 柳暗花明 is a sudden new way out appearing just when one seemed stuck.

cards.cue: Talks had been stuck for weeks and everyone expected failure; then one new proposal opened everything up again. How did things turn?

ctx.s: 正当我们以为没希望的时候，事情突然{柳暗花明}。
ctx.en: Just when we thought there was no hope, things suddenly opened up.

ctx.s: 找了半年工作都没结果，后来一位老同学推荐了他，总算{柳暗花明}。
ctx.en: Half a year of job hunting got him nowhere; then an old classmate recommended him and at last a way opened.

ctx.s: 谈判陷入僵局，对方第二天却提出了新方案，局面一下子{柳暗花明}。
ctx.en: The talks had reached deadlock, but the next day the other side proposed a new plan and the situation suddenly brightened.

ctx.s: “别灰心，说不定过几天就{柳暗花明}了。”
ctx.en: "Don't lose heart; in a few days a way out may well appear."

ctx.s: 研究卡住了好几个月，一次偶然的实验结果带来了{柳暗花明}的转机。
ctx.en: The research was stuck for months; a chance experimental result brought an unexpected way forward.

ctx.s: 本以为这次肯定失败了，没想到又有了转机，真是山重水复疑无路，{柳暗花明}又一村。
ctx.en: I was sure it had failed, but then things turned around: just when the road seemed to end, a new village came into view.

bad.s: 他一直很顺利，今天又{柳暗花明}了。
bad.en: (meant: things went well for him again today)
bad.why: It needs an apparent dead end first; for progress that has always been smooth, a different idiom about plain sailing fits.

bad.s: 公司倒闭了，大家都感到{柳暗花明}。
bad.en: (meant: everyone felt it was hopeless)
bad.why: It is the turn toward hope, not despair; a company collapsing with no way out is the opposite situation.

cards.mean: at a dead end with nowhere left to turn
cards.lit: walking, with no road left to head for

use.how: Predicate or attributive (走投无路的人); often 被逼得走投无路. Said of a person in desperate straits with no help or way out.

near.diff: 穷途末路 is the end of the road, often for a doomed person or force, and can sound critical; 走投无路 stresses having nowhere to turn for help.

cards.cue: Turned away by every bank and every relative, a man drowning in debt has no one left to ask. Describe his situation.

ctx.s: 他欠了很多钱，已经{走投无路}了。
ctx.en: He owes a lot of money and has nowhere left to turn.

ctx.s: 要不是{走投无路}，谁会去求人呢？
ctx.en: Who would go begging for help unless they had no other way out?

ctx.s: 那年她丢了工作又生了病，几乎{走投无路}。
ctx.en: That year she lost her job and fell ill, and was nearly at the end of her rope.

ctx.s: 被警察包围以后，小偷{走投无路}，只好投降。
ctx.en: Surrounded by the police, the thief had no way out and had to give himself up.

ctx.s: “你为什么来找我？”“我实在是{走投无路}了，只有你能帮我。”
ctx.en: "Why have you come to me?" "I really have nowhere else to turn; only you can help me."

ctx.s: 当年很多{走投无路}的农民只好离开家乡，到城里谋生。
ctx.en: Back then many desperate farmers had no choice but to leave home and seek a living in the cities.

bad.s: 这条小路{走投无路}，我们回去吧。
bad.en: (meant: this lane is a dead end, let's go back)
bad.why: It describes a person's desperate plight, not a road; a lane that leads nowhere is simply a dead end.

bad.s: 生活把他{走投无路}了。
bad.en: (meant: life drove him to despair)
bad.why: It is not a causative verb that takes an object; you must say life forced him (bi de) until he had nowhere to turn.

cards.mean: unable to stop once committed
cards.lit: riding a tiger, it is hard to get off

story.text: When Yang Jian was seizing power at the Northern Zhou court, his wife, later Empress Dugu, sent him word that the great undertaking was already under way: like someone riding a wild beast, he could not get down, so he must press on. He went on to found the Sui dynasty. The image of a rider who cannot dismount became this idiom.

use.how: Predicate, often 弄得骑虎难下 or 我也是骑虎难下. Said of someone who has started something and cannot back out without worse loss or loss of face.

near.diff: 进退两难 is any dilemma where both choices are hard; 骑虎难下 stresses that one has already committed and stopping would be worse.

cards.cue: He boasted he'd start a company; now friends have put money in and pulling out would humiliate him, though he regrets it. His position?

ctx.s: 话已经说出去了，现在他{骑虎难下}。
ctx.en: He has already said it publicly, and now he can't back down.

ctx.s: 投了这么多钱，项目停下来损失更大，公司{骑虎难下}。
ctx.en: So much money has gone in that stopping the project would cost even more; the company is stuck with it.

ctx.s: 他本来只是开玩笑说要跑马拉松，结果大家都当真了，弄得他{骑虎难下}。
ctx.en: He only joked about running a marathon, but everyone took him seriously, and now he can't back out.

ctx.s: “你为什么还在跟他们打官司？”“事情闹到这一步，我也是{骑虎难下}啊。”
ctx.en: "Why are you still suing them?" "It has gone this far; I can't just stop now."

ctx.s: 婚礼请帖都发出去了，她心里后悔，却{骑虎难下}。
ctx.en: The wedding invitations had all gone out; she regretted it inside but felt there was no backing out.

ctx.s: 双方都公开表了态，谁先让步谁就丢面子，现在谁都{骑虎难下}。
ctx.en: Both sides had taken public positions and whoever gave way first would lose face, so neither could back down.

bad.s: 他还没开始做这件事，所以{骑虎难下}。
bad.en: (meant: he hasn't started, so he can't decide)
bad.why: It needs a commitment already made; hesitating before you have even started is simple indecision.

bad.s: 这道题太难了，我{骑虎难下}。
bad.en: (meant: this problem is too hard for me to solve)
bad.why: It is about being unable to back out of something begun, not about a task being too difficult.

cards.mean: easily solved once the key is found
cards.lit: meeting the blade, it splits apart

story.text: During the Jin campaign against the state of Wu, some generals wanted to stop and wait. The commander Du Yu refused: the army's momentum, he said, was like splitting bamboo; once the first few joints are cut, the rest split apart as they meet the blade. He pressed on and Wu fell.

use.how: Predicate with the problem as subject, often after 就 or 都: 问题迎刃而解。 It takes no object.

near.diff: 轻而易举 says a task is easy to do; 迎刃而解 says problems fall away once the key one is dealt with.

cards.cue: Three bugs in an app all came from one wrong setting; once she fixed that setting, all three vanished at once. What happened to the bugs?

ctx.s: 找到原因以后，问题就{迎刃而解}了。
ctx.en: Once we found the cause, the problem solved itself.

ctx.s: 只要把基础打好，后面的难题都会{迎刃而解}。
ctx.en: As long as you build a solid foundation, the harder problems later will all fall into place.

ctx.s: 老师一句提示，我卡了半天的那道题就{迎刃而解}了。
ctx.en: With one hint from the teacher, the problem I'd been stuck on for ages was suddenly easy.

ctx.s: “两个部门一直吵来吵去，怎么办？”“让他们坐下来见一面，很多误会自然{迎刃而解}。”
ctx.en: "The two departments keep arguing; what should we do?" "Get them to sit down together, and many misunderstandings will clear up by themselves."

ctx.s: 资金一到位，招人、租房这些麻烦都{迎刃而解}。
ctx.en: Once the funding came through, hiring, renting space and all those headaches were sorted out at a stroke.

ctx.s: 专家指出，只要解决了人才问题，其他困难都将{迎刃而解}。
ctx.en: The experts point out that once the talent problem is solved, the other difficulties will resolve easily.

bad.s: 我{迎刃而解}了这个问题。
bad.en: (meant: I solved this problem)
bad.why: It takes no object and its subject is the problem itself: the problem resolves, rather than I resolve the problem.

bad.s: 这件事我们费了好几个月的劲，一点一点才{迎刃而解}。
bad.en: (meant: after months of hard work, bit by bit, we finally solved it)
bad.why: It means things resolve easily once the key is found, not after a long, laborious grind of many months.

cards.mean: admirable because it is so hard to do
cards.lit: hard to manage, and so worth prizing

use.how: Predicate (真是难能可贵) or attributive (难能可贵的精神). Praises a person's act or quality that is rare given how hard it is.

near.diff: 来之不易 says a result was hard-won and should be cherished; 难能可贵 praises the act or quality itself as admirably rare.

cards.cue: A single mother working two jobs still studies every night and finishes her degree. How do you praise her for managing something so rare?

ctx.s: 他这么年轻就这么有耐心，真是{难能可贵}。
ctx.en: For someone so young to be so patient is truly admirable.

ctx.s: 在那么困难的条件下坚持读完大学，{难能可贵}。
ctx.en: Sticking with university to the end under such hard conditions is really commendable.

ctx.s: 一个小孩子主动把捡到的钱交给警察，这种做法{难能可贵}。
ctx.en: A small child handing found money to the police on his own is something really to be valued.

ctx.s: “她每个周末都去养老院做志愿者，坚持了五年。”“这可真是{难能可贵}。”
ctx.en: "She has volunteered at the care home every weekend for five years." "That's truly admirable."

ctx.s: 比赛输了，他却第一个去向对手祝贺，这种风度{难能可贵}。
ctx.en: He lost the match but was the first to congratulate his opponent; that kind of sportsmanship is rare and admirable.

ctx.s: 评委认为，这部作品最{难能可贵}的是作者始终保持了真诚。
ctx.en: The judges felt that what is most admirable about this work is that the author stayed sincere throughout.

bad.s: 这件衣服很{难能可贵}，我买不起。
bad.en: (meant: this dress is very expensive, I can't afford it)
bad.why: It praises a person's admirable act or quality, not the price of a thing; for an expensive dress just say it is costly.

bad.s: 他偷懒不做作业，真是{难能可贵}。
bad.en: (meant: it's rare for him to slack off)
bad.why: It is praise for something admirable and hard to do; it cannot describe laziness or anything bad.

cards.mean: after hardship come the sweet times
cards.lit: the bitterness is used up, the sweetness arrives

use.how: Predicate, often with 终于 or 总算; also 苦尽甘来的一天. Said of a person or family whose long hardship has given way to good times.

near.diff: 柳暗花明 is a sudden way out of an impasse; 苦尽甘来 is a long stretch of hardship ending and good times following.

cards.cue: After years of night shifts and debt, a couple finally owns their home and their children are grown and doing well. Sum up their life now.

ctx.s: 熬了这么多年，他们家终于{苦尽甘来}了。
ctx.en: After all these hard years, their family's good times have finally come.

ctx.s: 她年轻时吃了很多苦，现在儿女都很孝顺，总算{苦尽甘来}。
ctx.en: She suffered a lot when she was young; now her children are devoted to her, and the sweet times have come at last.

ctx.s: “再坚持一下，等你毕业了就{苦尽甘来}了。”
ctx.en: "Hang in there a bit longer; once you graduate, the hard part will be over and the good times will come."

ctx.s: 经过多年艰苦创业，这家小工厂终于{苦尽甘来}，订单越来越多。
ctx.en: After years of hard struggle, the little factory has finally come through, with more and more orders.

ctx.s: 爷爷常说，人这一辈子总会有{苦尽甘来}的一天。
ctx.en: Grandpa often says that in every life the day comes when hardship ends and sweetness begins.

ctx.s: 这部电影讲的是一对穷苦夫妻相互扶持、{苦尽甘来}的故事。
ctx.en: The film tells the story of a poor couple who support each other until their hard times give way to happiness.

bad.s: 他从小家里有钱，一直很幸福，真是{苦尽甘来}。
bad.en: (meant: he has always had a happy, comfortable life)
bad.why: It needs a long period of hardship first; a life that was always comfortable has no bitterness to come to an end.

bad.s: 他终于{苦尽甘来}了他的生活。
bad.en: (meant: he finally ended the hardship of his life)
bad.why: It takes no object; the person or their life is the subject, as in: his life has finally come through the hard times.

cards.mean: a fleeting, short-lived success
cards.lit: the tan flower appears once: a bloom seen only briefly and rarely

story.text: The phrase goes back to the Lotus Sutra. The Buddha tells his disciple Shariputra that the buddhas teach this wonderful dharma only rarely, just as the udumbara flower (tan hua for short) appears only once in a very long time. Later the name came to be associated with the night-blooming cereus, whose flower opens for a few hours and then withers, and the phrase came to mean something brilliant that vanishes quickly.

use.how: Predicate or after 是/只是/不过是, about fame, success, a trend or a talent that shone and then faded: 他的走红只是昙花一现。

near.diff: 过眼云烟 says something passes and is not worth caring about; 昙花一现 stresses that a success or splendour was real but very short.

cards.cue: A singer had one viral hit, topped the charts for a month, and then disappeared from public view. How would you describe her fame?

ctx.s: 这家网红店火了一个月就关门了，真是{昙花一现}。
ctx.en: That trendy shop was the rage for a month and then closed down; its success didn't last at all.

ctx.s: 很多选秀歌手只是{昙花一现}，几年后就没人记得了。
ctx.en: Many talent-show singers are only a flash in the pan; a few years later nobody remembers them.

ctx.s: 他这次考了第一，你觉得会不会只是{昙花一现}？
ctx.en: He came first this time; do you think it might just be a one-off?

ctx.s: “这股热潮会持续吗？”“我看不过是{昙花一现}。”
ctx.en: "Will this craze last?" "I think it's just a passing flash."

ctx.s: 那位作家的成名作轰动一时，此后却再无佳作，他的辉煌如{昙花一现}。
ctx.en: That writer's breakthrough book caused a sensation, but nothing good followed; his glory was brief.

ctx.s: 要让改革的成果不至于{昙花一现}，关键在于建立长期机制。
ctx.en: To keep the results of the reform from being short-lived, the key is to build long-term mechanisms.

bad.s: 今天的会议{昙花一现}，只开了十分钟。
bad.en: (meant: today's meeting was very short, only ten minutes)
bad.why: It is about success or splendour that fades fast, not about an event simply being short.

bad.s: 这家老店开了一百年，生意一直{昙花一现}。
bad.en: (meant: this old shop has flourished for a hundred years)
bad.why: It means a brief glory that fades at once, so it cannot describe success that has lasted a century.

cards.mean: the place is the same but the people are gone
cards.lit: things are as they were, people are not

story.text: The phrase is best known from a lyric by the Song poet Li Qingzhao, written in her later years after her husband had died and she had fled south. After the wind has dropped and the blossoms have fallen, she writes: the things remain, the people have changed, everything is over; I want to speak, but tears come first.

use.how: Said with a sigh, as a comment or after 真是/已, when a familiar place or object remains but the people who belonged to it are gone or changed.

near.diff: 沧海桑田 is about the world itself changing completely over a long time; 物是人非 says the place stays and only the people are gone.

cards.cue: You return to your old school after twenty years: the buildings are exactly the same, but none of the people you knew are there.

ctx.s: 回到小时候住的院子，邻居都搬走了，真是{物是人非}。
ctx.en: I went back to the courtyard where I lived as a child; the neighbours have all moved away. Nothing has changed but the people.

ctx.s: 母校的教学楼还在，老师们却都退休了，{物是人非}啊。
ctx.en: My old school's buildings are still there, but the teachers have all retired. The place is the same, the people are gone.

ctx.s: 奶奶去世后再回老家，院子里那棵树还在，却已{物是人非}。
ctx.en: Going back home after Grandma died, the tree in the yard was still there, but she was not.

ctx.s: “你还去那家咖啡馆吗？”“不去了，{物是人非}，去了只会难过。”
ctx.en: "Do you still go to that café?" "No. It's the same place, but the people are gone; going would just make me sad."

ctx.s: 他翻看着十年前的合影，照片里的地方都还在，人却散了，不禁感慨{物是人非}。
ctx.en: Looking through a group photo from ten years ago, he saw the places were all still there but the people had scattered, and he sighed at how things had changed.

ctx.s: 小说结尾，主人公重返故乡，心中满是{物是人非}的感慨。
ctx.en: At the end of the novel the hero returns home, full of sorrow that the place remains while the people are gone.

bad.s: 新公司装修得很漂亮，跟以前完全不一样，真是{物是人非}。
bad.en: (meant: the new office looks completely different)
bad.why: It needs the place to stay the same while the people are gone; here the place itself changed and nobody is missing.

bad.s: 他换了个新发型，我差点认不出来，真是{物是人非}。
bad.en: (meant: he looks so different)
bad.why: It is a wistful sigh about lost people and times, not a remark on someone's changed appearance.

cards.mean: (of a task or problem) so pressing it cannot wait a moment
cards.lit: not even a moment allows delay

use.how: Predicate after a task or action, or before 的事: 抢修工作刻不容缓。 Said of what must be done; not used for a person acting hastily.

near.diff: 当务之急 is a noun naming the most urgent task (当务之急是…); 刻不容缓 is a predicate saying a task cannot wait.
迫在眉睫 pictures a danger or need already right before one's eyes; 刻不容缓 says the action must not be put off even a moment.

cards.cue: A dam above a town is cracking, and engineers warn that any delay could be fatal. How urgent is the repair work?

ctx.s: 病人大出血，手术{刻不容缓}。
ctx.en: The patient is haemorrhaging; the operation cannot wait a moment.

ctx.s: 河堤出现了裂缝，抢修工作{刻不容缓}，一分钟也不能耽误。
ctx.en: Cracks have appeared in the dyke; the emergency repairs must start at once, without losing a single minute.

ctx.s: 服务器被攻击了，修补漏洞{刻不容缓}。
ctx.en: The server has been attacked; patching the hole can't wait.

ctx.s: “这件事能不能等到下周？”“不能，这是{刻不容缓}的事。”
ctx.en: "Can this wait until next week?" "No, this has to be done right now."

ctx.s: 时间就是生命，救人{刻不容缓}，搜救队连夜出发了。
ctx.en: Every second counts: rescuing people couldn't wait a moment, so the search team set off that very night.

ctx.s: 灾区急需饮用水，救援物资的运送{刻不容缓}。
ctx.en: The disaster area urgently needs drinking water; getting relief supplies there cannot wait.

bad.s: 他饿坏了，{刻不容缓}地吃完了一大碗面。
bad.en: (meant: he was starving and wolfed down a big bowl of noodles)
bad.why: It describes a task that must not be delayed, not a person doing something eagerly or hurriedly.

bad.s: 这件事{刻不容缓}，我们下个月再讨论吧。
bad.en: (meant: this matter is important, let's discuss it next month)
bad.why: Saying something cannot wait a moment and then postponing it to next month contradicts the idiom.

cards.mean: the top priority right now
cards.lit: the urgent one among the tasks at hand

story.text: Mencius said that the wise know everything, yet treat the tasks that matter most at the present moment as the urgent ones; and the benevolent love everyone, yet put first the urgent work of being close to worthy people. Even a sage, he argued, cannot do all things at once and must choose what comes first.

use.how: A noun phrase, usually as subject in 当务之急是…, or after 是/才是: 现在的当务之急是找到资金。

near.diff: 刻不容缓 is a predicate (这件事刻不容缓); 当务之急 is a noun naming which task comes first (当务之急是…).

cards.cue: Your startup has a dozen problems, but paying this month's salaries must be dealt with before any of them. Name that task.

ctx.s: 刚搬进新家，{当务之急}是把网络装好。
ctx.en: We've just moved in; the first thing to sort out is the internet.

ctx.s: 公司现金流快断了，{当务之急}是先找到资金。
ctx.en: The company is about to run out of cash; the most urgent thing is to find money.

ctx.s: 你现在的{当务之急}不是玩游戏，而是准备下周的考试。
ctx.en: Your priority right now isn't gaming, it's preparing for next week's exam.

ctx.s: “我们该先做什么？”“{当务之急}是联系上孩子的家长。”
ctx.en: "What should we do first?" "The most urgent thing is to get hold of the child's parents."

ctx.s: 对这座老城来说，修复排水系统才是{当务之急}。
ctx.en: For this old city, repairing the drainage system is what matters most right now.

ctx.s: 他意识到，比起换工作，把身体养好才是自己的{当务之急}。
ctx.en: He realised that, more than changing jobs, getting his health back was his real priority.

bad.s: 这件事很{当务之急}，你快去办吧。
bad.en: (meant: this is very urgent, go and do it)
bad.why: It is a noun, not an adjective, so it cannot take hen; say the matter is urgent (hen ji), or call it the top priority with shi.

bad.s: 十年后买一套大房子是我的{当务之急}。
bad.en: (meant: buying a big house in ten years is my main goal)
bad.why: It means the most pressing task right now, so it cannot name a goal ten years away.

cards.mean: forced to by circumstances
cards.lit: pressed so that one cannot stop

use.how: Adverbial before a verb (迫不得已才…), or as predicate (是迫不得已的). Often used to justify an unwelcome choice someone had no way to avoid.

near.diff: 迫不及待 means too eager to wait; 迫不得已 means forced against one's wishes. They look alike but are near opposites in feeling.
身不由己 is an ongoing state of not being one's own master; 迫不得已 is about one particular choice forced by circumstances.

cards.cue: The last train has gone and you hate spending money, but you have no other way home than an expensive taxi. Explain why you took it.

ctx.s: 末班车走了，我{迫不得已}打车回家。
ctx.en: The last bus had gone, so I had no choice but to take a taxi home.

ctx.s: 要不是{迫不得已}，谁愿意离开家乡去外地打工？
ctx.en: Who would leave home to work far away unless they had to?

ctx.s: 房租涨得太厉害，老板{迫不得已}才关了这家餐厅。
ctx.en: The rent went up so much that the owner was forced to close the restaurant.

ctx.s: “你为什么卖掉那辆车？”“{迫不得已}，家里急需用钱。”
ctx.en: "Why did you sell that car?" "I had no choice; the family needed money urgently."

ctx.s: 这么做实在是{迫不得已}，希望大家理解。
ctx.en: We really had no alternative; we hope everyone understands.

ctx.s: 由于暴雨，主办方{迫不得已}将演唱会改到下个月。
ctx.en: Because of the rainstorm, the organisers were forced to move the concert to next month.

bad.s: 放假了，我{迫不得已}想见到你。
bad.en: (meant: now it's the holidays, I can't wait to see you)
bad.why: Being too eager to wait is po bu ji dai; po bu de yi means doing something against one's will.

bad.s: 这家的饺子太好吃了，我{迫不得已}吃了三盘。
bad.en: (meant: the dumplings were so good I couldn't help eating three plates)
bad.why: Not being able to resist something pleasant is ren bu zhu; this idiom means being forced by bad circumstances.

cards.mean: not in control of one's own actions
cards.lit: the body does not follow oneself

use.how: Predicate or adverbial (身不由己地…). Said when a role, job, situation or physical force decides what one does; often as an excuse: 人在江湖，身不由己。

near.diff: 迫不得已 is one forced choice at one moment; 身不由己 describes a situation where one is not one's own master at all.

cards.cue: Your job keeps forcing you into things you don't want to do, like drinking at business dinners. How do you describe your position?

ctx.s: 地铁里人太多，我被挤得{身不由己}，一直往后退。
ctx.en: The metro was so packed that I was pushed backwards and couldn't stop myself.

ctx.s: 他也不想天天加班，可在这个岗位上{身不由己}。
ctx.en: He doesn't want to work late every day either, but in that position he has no say.

ctx.s: “你怎么又喝醉了？”“应酬嘛，{身不由己}。”
ctx.en: "Drunk again?" "Business dinners. It's not up to me."

ctx.s: 当上经理以后，她常常感到{身不由己}，连休假都要看公司安排。
ctx.en: Since becoming a manager she often feels she isn't her own master; even her holidays depend on the company.

ctx.s: 电影里的卧底警察说：“我做的很多事都是{身不由己}。”
ctx.en: The undercover cop in the film says, "Much of what I did, I had no control over."

ctx.s: 那段日子，他被卷进家族的纷争，{身不由己}地站到了父亲那边。
ctx.en: In those days he was dragged into the family feud and found himself, against his will, on his father's side.

bad.s: 今天没有安排，我{身不由己}，想去哪儿就去哪儿。
bad.en: (meant: I'm free today and can go wherever I like)
bad.why: It means the opposite: not being free to decide what one does.

bad.s: 我发烧了，全身{身不由己}，很难受。
bad.en: (meant: I have a fever and feel awful all over)
bad.why: It is about one's actions being controlled by circumstances, not about feeling physically unwell.

cards.mean: just as one pleases
cards.lit: following the heart in whatever it wants

story.text: The idiom is traced to Confucius's summary of his own life in the Analects: at fifteen he set his heart on learning, at thirty he stood firm, and so on, until at seventy he could follow what his heart desired without overstepping the rules. The modern idiom keeps the first half, following the heart, and drops the rule-keeping.

use.how: Adverbial (随心所欲地…) or predicate. Freedom to act as one likes; neutral or positive, and negative only after 不能/别: 钱不能随心所欲地花。

near.diff: 为所欲为 is always condemnation of doing wrong without restraint; 随心所欲 is just freedom to act as one likes, often a good thing.

cards.cue: It's the first day of the holidays: no alarm, no schedule, and you can do whatever you feel like all day.

ctx.s: 放假了，终于可以{随心所欲}地睡懒觉。
ctx.en: The holidays are here; at last I can sleep in as much as I like.

ctx.s: 这款软件可以让你{随心所欲}地调整页面布局。
ctx.en: This software lets you adjust the page layout however you like.

ctx.s: “旅行要不要做计划？”“我喜欢{随心所欲}，走到哪儿算哪儿。”
ctx.en: "Do you plan your trips?" "I like to go wherever I feel like and see where I end up."

ctx.s: 钱不是大风刮来的，你不能这样{随心所欲}地花。
ctx.en: Money doesn't grow on trees; you can't just spend it however you please.

ctx.s: 写初稿时可以{随心所欲}，修改时再讲究结构。
ctx.en: In a first draft you can write freely; worry about structure when you revise.

ctx.s: 他的书法已到了{随心所欲}的境界，每一笔都自然而有分寸。
ctx.en: His calligraphy has reached the stage where he writes freely, every stroke natural yet controlled.

bad.s: “我们去哪家餐厅？”“{随心所欲}！”
bad.en: (meant: "Which restaurant?" "Whatever you like!")
bad.why: It describes how someone acts, not a reply handing the choice to the other person; say sui ni or ting ni de.

bad.s: 他这次考试{随心所欲}，考了满分。
bad.en: (meant: the exam went just as he hoped and he got full marks)
bad.why: It means acting freely, not results turning out as hoped; for that say ru yuan yi chang or xin xiang shi cheng.

cards.mean: to do whatever one likes, however wrong
cards.lit: to do whatever one wishes to do

use.how: Intransitive predicate, often after 可以/敢/不能: 别以为有钱就可以为所欲为。 Condemns someone, usually with money or power, who ignores rules and others.

near.diff: 随心所欲 is neutral freedom to do as one likes; 为所欲为 condemns doing wrong because nothing stops one.
肆无忌惮 stresses brazenness and usually modifies a specific act (肆无忌惮地…); 为所欲为 says someone does whatever they like.

cards.cue: The boss's nephew ignores every company rule, bullies staff and takes what he wants, and nobody dares to stop him.

ctx.s: 别以为有钱就可以{为所欲为}。
ctx.en: Don't think that having money means you can do whatever you want.

ctx.s: 那个经理仗着老板是他舅舅，在公司里{为所欲为}。
ctx.en: That manager, relying on the boss being his uncle, does whatever he likes in the company.

ctx.s: “他凭什么想罚款就罚款？”“没人管他，他当然敢{为所欲为}。”
ctx.en: "What right does he have to fine people whenever he likes?" "Nobody keeps him in check, so of course he does as he pleases."

ctx.s: 法律的存在，就是为了不让任何人{为所欲为}。
ctx.en: Laws exist precisely so that no one can do whatever they like.

ctx.s: 这个小区的物业缺少监督，长期{为所欲为}，业主怨声载道。
ctx.en: The estate's management company has no oversight and has done as it pleased for years; the residents are furious.

ctx.s: 故事里的恶霸在镇上{为所欲为}，直到新县令到任。
ctx.en: In the story the local bully did whatever he wanted in the town until the new magistrate arrived.

bad.s: 老师鼓励我们{为所欲为}，大胆发挥创造力。
bad.en: (meant: the teacher encouraged us to be free and creative)
bad.why: It always condemns wrongdoing, so no teacher would encourage it; say zi you fa hui or sui xin suo yu.

bad.s: 他{为所欲为}了这家公司。
bad.en: (meant: he did whatever he wanted with this company)
bad.why: It takes no object; put the place before it with zai: he does as he likes in the company.

cards.mean: brazenly, without any restraint
cards.lit: unbridled, with nothing feared or held back

use.how: Mostly adverbial before a specific act (肆无忌惮地骂人/排污), sometimes predicate. Condemns behaviour done openly with no regard for rules or others.

near.diff: 为所欲为 says someone does whatever they like in general; 肆无忌惮 stresses the brazen, open manner of a particular act.

cards.cue: In a quiet library, a man shouts into his phone for twenty minutes, ignoring the glares of everyone around him.

ctx.s: 他在图书馆里{肆无忌惮}地大声打电话。
ctx.en: He was talking loudly on the phone in the library without the slightest regard for anyone.

ctx.s: 有些网友躲在屏幕后面，{肆无忌惮}地辱骂别人。
ctx.en: Some people hide behind their screens and insult others with complete brazenness.

ctx.s: 这家工厂{肆无忌惮}地往河里排放污水。
ctx.en: This factory openly dumps waste water into the river without any scruple.

ctx.s: 小偷竟然在大白天{肆无忌惮}地撬车门。
ctx.en: The thief brazenly forced car doors open in broad daylight.

ctx.s: “他怎么敢这样跟老师说话？”“仗着他爸是校长，越来越{肆无忌惮}了。”
ctx.en: "How dare he talk to the teacher like that?" "His dad's the head, so he's getting more and more brazen."

ctx.s: 文章批评了某些商家{肆无忌惮}地夸大宣传、欺骗消费者的做法。
ctx.en: The article criticised some businesses for shamelessly exaggerating their claims and deceiving consumers.

bad.s: 他{肆无忌惮}地努力学习，每天学到半夜。
bad.en: (meant: he studied with total dedication until midnight)
bad.why: It condemns brazen wrongdoing; it cannot describe hard work.

bad.s: 消防员{肆无忌惮}地冲进火场救人。
bad.en: (meant: the firefighters fearlessly rushed into the fire)
bad.why: Fearless courage deserves praise, such as fen bu gu shen; this idiom means flouting rules and would insult them.

cards.mean: with no turning back, for what one knows is right
cards.lit: duty allows no looking back

story.text: The wording goes back to the Han writer Sima Xiangru's proclamation to the people of Ba and Shu. He praised the men of the border regions who, at the first alarm, took up their bows and ran to fight, facing bare blades and flying arrows: duty would not let them look back, nor their resolve let them turn on their heels. His wording was yi bu fan gu; the bu (not) later became wu (no).

use.how: Mostly adverbial (义无反顾地…) before a committed act: going, joining, standing up. Praises someone who goes ahead for a just cause despite cost or danger.

near.diff: 一意孤行 criticises stubbornly going one's own way against advice; 义无反顾 praises going ahead because it is right.

cards.cue: Knowing she will lose her well-paid job, a nurse still volunteers for a dangerous rescue mission because it is the right thing to do.

ctx.s: 听说家乡发生地震，他{义无反顾}地回去当志愿者。
ctx.en: Hearing of the earthquake in his hometown, he went straight back to volunteer without a second thought.

ctx.s: 她放弃了高薪工作，{义无反顾}地投身乡村教育。
ctx.en: She gave up a well-paid job and devoted herself to rural education without looking back.

ctx.s: “你想清楚了吗？”“想清楚了，这条路我会{义无反顾}地走下去。”
ctx.en: "Have you thought it through?" "I have. I'll follow this path to the end, whatever it costs."

ctx.s: 明知揭发真相会丢掉工作，他还是{义无反顾}地站了出来。
ctx.en: He knew exposing the truth would cost him his job, yet he stood up without hesitation.

ctx.s: 疫情最严重的时候，许多医生{义无反顾}地奔赴一线。
ctx.en: At the worst of the epidemic, many doctors went resolutely to the front line.

ctx.s: 小说中的主人公为了救出朋友，{义无反顾}地冲进了燃烧的大楼。
ctx.en: In the novel, the hero rushes into the burning building without hesitation to save his friend.

bad.s: 他输光了钱，还是{义无反顾}地去赌博。
bad.en: (meant: even after losing everything, he still went on gambling)
bad.why: It praises resolve for a just cause; for persisting in a vice say zhi mi bu wu or lu jiao bu gai.

bad.s: 他{义无反顾}地往前走，没听见我在后面叫他。
bad.en: (meant: he walked on without looking back and didn't hear me calling)
bad.why: Looking back here means moral hesitation, not literally turning round; it is not about walking on without looking behind.

cards.mean: to stake everything on one last gamble
cards.lit: to throw the last stake in a single cast of the dice

story.text: In gambling, a player who had nearly lost everything and pushed all he had left onto the table was said to make a 'lone stake' (guzhu), his last one. In the Song dynasty, the official Wang Qinruo told Emperor Zhenzong that when the minister Kou Zhun urged him to go to the front at Chanyuan, Kou Zhun had used the emperor himself as his last stake. The emperor's favour towards Kou Zhun cooled after this.

use.how: Predicate or adverbial, often with 决定 or 只好: 他决定孤注一掷。 Said of a risky all-or-nothing move made when other options are gone; often slightly critical.

near.diff: 破釜沉舟 praises cutting off one's own retreat to fight with total resolve; 孤注一掷 stresses betting everything on one risky chance.

cards.cue: Down to his last savings, a man puts every cent into one risky venture: if it fails, he has nothing left. What is he doing?

ctx.s: 他把全部积蓄都拿去开店，真是{孤注一掷}。
ctx.en: He put all his savings into opening a shop: a real all-or-nothing bet.

ctx.s: 比赛只剩最后一分钟，教练决定{孤注一掷}，让守门员也上前进攻。
ctx.en: With one minute left, the coach decided to go for broke and sent even the goalkeeper forward.

ctx.s: “你真要把房子卖了去创业？”“没别的办法了，只能{孤注一掷}。”
ctx.en: "You're really selling the house to start a business?" "There's no other way; I have to risk it all."

ctx.s: 公司濒临破产，老板{孤注一掷}，把最后的资金全部投进了新产品。
ctx.en: With the company near bankruptcy, the boss staked everything, pouring the last of the money into a new product.

ctx.s: 投资需要冷静，千万不要在亏损之后{孤注一掷}。
ctx.en: Investing needs a cool head; never bet everything on one throw after a loss.

ctx.s: 敌军被围多日，粮草将尽，终于{孤注一掷}，趁夜突围。
ctx.en: Surrounded for days and almost out of supplies, the enemy finally made a desperate all-out bid to break out by night.

bad.s: 我周末{孤注一掷}，去看了一场电影。
bad.en: (meant: I decided on a whim to see a film at the weekend)
bad.why: It means risking everything one has on one chance; seeing a film risks nothing.

bad.s: 他学习很稳定，每次考试都{孤注一掷}地拿高分。
bad.en: (meant: he steadily gets high marks in every exam)
bad.why: It describes a desperate one-off gamble, not steady, reliable success.

cards.mean: to believe firmly without a doubt
cards.lit: to believe deeply and not doubt

use.how: Predicate, usually with 对……深信不疑 or followed by a clause: 他对这件事深信不疑。 Said of a person's belief in a claim, a person or an idea, true or false.

near.diff: 信以为真 is taking something false to be true, usually a trick or rumour; 深信不疑 is just firm belief, which may well be right.

cards.cue: Everyone tells her the plan won't work, but she has no doubt at all that it will. How would you describe her belief?

ctx.s: 孩子们对圣诞老人的存在{深信不疑}。
ctx.en: The children believe without a doubt that Father Christmas exists.

ctx.s: 他对自己的判断{深信不疑}，谁劝都不听。
ctx.en: He is completely sure of his own judgement and won't listen to anyone.

ctx.s: 奶奶对这个偏方{深信不疑}，每天都按时喝。
ctx.en: Grandma has total faith in this folk remedy and drinks it at the same time every day.

ctx.s: “你怎么那么肯定他是无辜的？”“我了解他，对此{深信不疑}。”
ctx.en: "How can you be so sure he's innocent?" "I know him; I have no doubt about it."

ctx.s: 经过多次实验，他对这个结论{深信不疑}。
ctx.en: After many experiments, he had no doubt at all about this conclusion.

ctx.s: 他始终{深信不疑}：只要坚持下去，总会成功。
ctx.en: He firmly believed throughout that if he kept going, he would succeed in the end.

bad.s: 我{深信不疑}他会不会来，所以一直在等。
bad.en: (meant: I wasn't sure whether he would come)
bad.why: It expresses complete certainty, so it cannot frame an open question about whether he will come.

bad.s: 这个朋友很{深信不疑}，你可以放心。
bad.en: (meant: this friend is very trustworthy)
bad.why: It describes a person who believes, not a person who deserves trust; nor can it be modified by 'very'.

cards.mean: to turn a blind eye
cards.lit: to look but not see

story.text: The phrase comes from the Confucian classic The Great Learning, which says that when the mind is not present, one looks but does not see, listens but does not hear, and eats but does not know the taste. There it describes inattention; today it usually means deliberately ignoring something one ought to deal with.

use.how: Predicate, often 对……视而不见: 老师对作弊视而不见。 Criticises ignoring a problem, a person or a fact that is plainly there.

near.diff: 置之不理 is leaving a request or matter unanswered; 视而不见 stresses pretending not to notice something in plain sight.

cards.cue: Litter has been piling up by the office door for weeks; everyone walks past it every day as if it weren't there. What are they doing?

ctx.s: 地上那么多垃圾，大家却都{视而不见}。
ctx.en: There's so much rubbish on the floor, yet everyone acts as if they don't see it.

ctx.s: 孩子在学校被欺负，老师怎么能{视而不见}呢？
ctx.en: A child is being bullied at school: how can the teacher turn a blind eye?

ctx.s: 这些违规就发生在管理人员眼皮底下，他们却长期{视而不见}。
ctx.en: These violations happened right under the managers' noses, yet for years they turned a blind eye.

ctx.s: “他又迟到了。”“经理好像一直{视而不见}。”
ctx.en: "He's late again." "The manager always seems to look the other way."

ctx.s: 对自己的缺点{视而不见}，是很难进步的。
ctx.en: If you ignore your own faults, it's very hard to improve.

ctx.s: 他找了半天钥匙，其实钥匙就在桌上，他却{视而不见}。
ctx.en: He searched for his keys for ages, though they were right on the table; he just looked straight past them.

bad.s: 天太黑了，我{视而不见}前面的路。
bad.en: (meant: it was too dark for me to see the road ahead)
bad.why: It is about ignoring what can be seen, not about being unable to see in the dark; use 'cannot see' instead.

bad.s: 他对朋友的成功{视而不见}，真是一个谦虚的人。
bad.en: (meant: he is modest about his friend's success)
bad.why: It is criticism for ignoring something one should notice; it cannot be used to praise modesty.

cards.mean: to give up on oneself
cards.lit: to ruin oneself and abandon oneself

story.text: Mencius said that one cannot reason with those who ruin themselves, nor do anything worthwhile with those who abandon themselves. To speak against propriety and righteousness he called ruining oneself; to say 'I cannot live by benevolence and righteousness' he called abandoning oneself.

use.how: Predicate, very often after 不要 or 开始: 别因为一次失败就自暴自弃。 Said of a person who stops trying and lets themselves go, usually after a setback.

near.diff: 破罐破摔 is colloquial and blunter, making things worse on purpose since they are already bad; 自暴自弃 is neutral to formal, losing hope in oneself.

cards.cue: After failing the entrance exam, a boy stops studying, sleeps all day and says he is worthless anyway. What is his friend warning him against?

ctx.s: 一次考试没考好，不要{自暴自弃}。
ctx.en: You did badly in one exam: don't give up on yourself.

ctx.s: 失业以后，他开始{自暴自弃}，整天喝酒。
ctx.en: After losing his job he gave up on himself and drank all day.

ctx.s: “我什么都做不好。”“别这么说，你可不能{自暴自弃}啊！”
ctx.en: "I can't do anything right." "Don't say that, you mustn't give up on yourself!"

ctx.s: 受伤后的那段日子，她差点{自暴自弃}，是家人把她拉了回来。
ctx.en: In the months after her injury she nearly gave up on herself; her family pulled her back.

ctx.s: 面对挫折，有人奋起，有人{自暴自弃}。
ctx.en: Faced with setbacks, some people rise up and others give up on themselves.

ctx.s: 老师相信，只要他不{自暴自弃}，一定还有机会。
ctx.en: The teacher believes that as long as he doesn't give up on himself, he still has a chance.

bad.s: 天气太热，我们{自暴自弃}了爬山的计划。
bad.en: (meant: we gave up our hiking plan because of the heat)
bad.why: It means losing hope in oneself, not dropping a plan, and it takes no object such as a plan.

bad.s: 他为了救别人，{自暴自弃}地冲进了火里。
